stimuli.description: A modern interior office room of dimensions 4.0 m × 7.4 m x 3.0 m. Participants experienced the virtual office environment from a seated position at a desk, and were able to look around freely to see various aspects of the room. 17 different artificial lighting conditions were tested, varying in illuminance (300lm to 4500lm) and CCT (1500 K to 7500 K).

tables.description: Top 3 correlations and their linear regression results for both illumination and CCT.
key_stats: ILLUMINATION Correlation: α/θ.C4 (r=0.95, p=0.001), α/θ.P4 (r=0.94, p=0.002), β/θ.PZ (r=0.91, p=0.005)
ILLUMINATION Linear Regression: α/θ.C4 (F[1, 47.15], Adj R²=0.88, p=0.001), α/θ.P4 (F[1, 37.93], Adj R²=0.86, p=0.002), β/θ.PZ (F[1, 22.65], Adj R²=0.78, p=0.005)

limitations: The range of luminance that VR HMDs can produce is still limited compared to real-world light sources, diminishing usefulness at extremes of very high and very low illuminance.
The VR experience does not accurately reflect blinding effects or glare from real-world lighting sources.

HMDs' minimum displayable intensities are too high to elicit a user's full scotopic vision range, making reliable study of color shifts and diminished visual acuity in very low-light environments impossible.
Caution should be used when generalizing study findings to non-virtual environments.
Higher-than-expected attrition rate due to loss of data from multiple participants (corrupted/unusable EEG data, missing timestamps, technical issues with HMD/EEG battery crashes, human error).
Convenience sample composed mostly of undergraduate students at Cornell University.
Demographic variables or other factors (e.g., participant sleep schedules or time of day) that may impact results were not evaluated.
